# The Bet · FinWise

> Module 1 · Ignite a PLG Motion. The growth hypothesis and where you're betting, plus the growth-loop visualization.

## Growth hypothesis

FinWise's biggest growth problem is FinWise is losing customers faster than it gains them, and adding acquisition spend no longer helps., because We believe customers churn because FinWise stays a single-user tool, used by one person who can easily abandon it. When a second person, such as an accountant, bookkeeper or teammate, works in the same account, FinWise becomes shared infrastructure, and leaving means moving two people's workflow.  We also believe invited collaborators are higher-quality users than paid traffic. They arrive through someone they trust, with a real task to do, so they should start trials and convert at higher rates.  If both are true, a collaboration loop improves retention and brings in better users at the same time.  Assumption to confirm first: FinWise supports multiple users per account, and there's a natural reason to share, such as an accountant reviewing the books..

_Working notes: I think Finwise's biggest problem is their bucket leaks faster than it fills e.g. they loose active users quicker or at the same rate than they can activate them. Evidence: The FinWise scenario
You are a PM at FinWise Co., a SaaS company providing financial-management software to small businesses. FinWise recently reached product-market fit and wants to focus heavily on growth and distribution over the next year. They use a product-led growth approach with a reverse-trial experience, aiming to make the product compelling enough to convert users into paid customers. Currently:
Only 2% of customers who begin a trial convert to paying customers
Annual Recurring Revenue is $10M
One-year retention for paid customers is 40%, meaning 60% churn within a year
Most of the marketing budget goes to paid acquisition to drive trial sign-ups
Adding more money to acquisition is no longer driving meaningful growth Against the data: 1. The trial is where FinWise loses the most people, proportionally.
6,424 trials became 128 paid customers. 98.0% of trialists didn't convert.

2. More traffic doesn't produce more trials.
June 2024 had the most visits (9,426) and the fewest trials (321, a 3.4% rate). July had among the fewest visits (5,466) and an 11.2% rate. Visits and trials barely correlate (0.09).

3. FinWise is losing customers faster than it gains them.
317 churned against 128 new paid customers, and churn exceeded new paid in all 13 months.

4. Trial-to-paid conversion data isn't usable.
Paid equals Trials × 2%, rounded, in every month. Nothing can be learned from that column.

Updated thinking

Retention moves from "first priority" to "urgent". Earlier I argued for fixing the leaky bucket before growth. The data makes the case stronger: at 2.5 churned customers for every new one, extra acquisition can't outrun the losses.

The acquisition problem looks like a traffic-quality problem. The scenario said extra paid spend isn't driving growth. The data shows the same thing one step earlier: visit volume doesn't predict trial starts. That points more toward which visitors we're buying than how many. It's still a hypothesis, since the data has no channel breakdown.

The activation hypothesis is untested, not wrong. We can't tell whether the 98% never got started or tried the product and declined to pay. It stays a live bet, but we can't build on it yet.

So the first action changes. Instead of a funnel test, the first step is fixing the data:

Real, user-level trial tracking: activity during the trial and actual conversion, not a modelled 2%.
Acquisition channel on every visit and trial, to test the traffic-quality idea.
A clear churn definition tied to cohorts, so we know which customers are leaving and when.

Without these, every bet we've discussed rests on assumptions the data can't check._

## The bet

Design: randomised A/B test on new trial accounts.  Control: current trial experience, no invite prompt. Variant: a prompt to invite an accountant, bookkeeper or teammate at a natural moment in the workflow, such as after the user first imports data or prepares something an accountant would need to review.  Duration: 8 weeks of trial enrolment, with retention tracked out to 6 months for anyone who converts.  Primary metric: 6-month retention for paid accounts in the variant vs. control.  Secondary metrics:  Invite rate: % of variant accounts sending at least one invite. Acceptance rate: % of invites accepted. Trial-to-paid conversion in variant vs. control. Loop output: new trials started by invited users, and their conversion rate compared with paid-acquisition sign-ups.  Guardrail: trial completion and conversion rate, to make sure the prompt doesn't add friction that loses users.  Success: variant accounts retain meaningfully better than control, and invited users convert at a higher rate than paid sign-ups.  Kill criteria:  Fewer than about 10% of accounts invite anyone. The loop doesn't exist for this product. Collaborative accounts don't retain better than single-user ones. Collaboration isn't the retention lever.  Prerequisite: user-level tracking of invites, trial activity, actual conversion and retention. The current data can't measure any of these.

Variant: a prompt to invite an accountant, bookkeeper or teammate at a natural moment in the workflow, such as after the user first imports data or prepares something an accountant would need to review.

Trial-to-paid conversion in variant vs. control.

Guardrail: trial completion and conversion rate, to make sure the prompt doesn't add friction that loses users.

Success: variant accounts retain meaningfully better than control, and invited users convert at a higher rate than paid sign-ups.

Kill criteria:

Fewer than about 10% of accounts invite anyone. The loop doesn't exist for this product.
Collaborative accounts don't retain better than single-user ones. Collaboration isn't the retention lever.

Prerequisite: user-level tracking of invites, trial activity, actual conversion and retention. The current data can't measure any of these.

## Growth loop

**Loop type:** Collaboration, It's the only one of the three that works on both problems the data showed: churn and traffic quality.
